utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer with Matthew Olmsted, Case Manager Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go into private session for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform you that one of Defence exhibits, it is D16, was admitted into evidence just in English version, in English translation. Somehow original -- B/C/S original was omitted. It is a judgement of War Crime Chamber of the High Court in Belgrade from the Lovas case and it could be found in e-court under doc ID 1D002203. And I just like to -- to put it in the record so that the Trial Chamber could instruct the Registrar to put the original of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So of the English version already is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- and now we can have the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure -- I believe that I have in mind the same document or judgement that counsel has just referred to. Prosecution position -- I don't know if this is -- I believe this has not yet been admitted and there was an issue as to whether it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is a Defence exhibit number. Is it MFI'd, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document has been admitted into evidence as Defence Exhibit D16 on 26th of November through Witness Cirba, Zeljko. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have another judgement in mind for which we will be filing a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the original can be admitted as well, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rendulic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now could you state your name and your date of birth for the record, please. And give -- give your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Adam Rendulic, 19 November 1947. Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You will to make a solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that making that declaration you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you now read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it your witness, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rendulic.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to begin by asking you a few questions about your background. Can you tell us, where do you currently live?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I live in Lovas, where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how are you employed?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I am still director of the agricultural co-operative in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And is it correct that after high school you received an agricultural degree from Banja Luka university?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's where I graduated from the higher school of agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after completing university, did you return to Lovas in about 1969?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to Lovas in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did you begin working?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. First I went to do my military service in Pozarevac and then I returned from Pozarevac in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And where did you begin working when you returned to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I started working immediately in the agricultural co-operative in Lovas in December 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when did you become director of that co-operative?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I became director in 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I just want to check the date. You said 1975?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, 1985. 1985 I became director.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No problem. Can you tell -- oh, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I became director in 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's make sure we just have this correct. Is director the same as general manager?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you started in 1969, you were not the general manager?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, no. I became general manager in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think that clarifies that. Now, could you tell us a little bit about this co-operative back in 1990, 1991, what it did, and how big it was.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The agricultural co-operative of Lovas was mainly engaged in farming and organising our co-operators. We had about 1900 hectares and we had about 82 staff members. We organised our co-operants by financing and giving them loans; and, later on, we organised our own production, including vineyards and orchards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what were the ethnicities of the staff at the co-operative?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They were mainly Croats, plus a few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And have you ever held any political office?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And have you been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we bring up P233.140. This is tab 33. Your Honours, I think this was originally tendered under seal but I don't believe there is any reason for it to be under seal. So I think we can go ahead and broadcast it. I don't know if we have removed that designation. It has been indicated to me that we have not removed that designation, so the Prosecution would move at this time to remove the under seal designation of this exhibit. There really is no reason, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll have to believe you on this one, Mr. Olmsted, because we can't verify for the moment. But if you say there is no problem, the -- the -- confidential status will be lifted. Please do so, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could zoom in to the area that's south-west -- or south-east of Vukovar. It's kind of the little bit that sticks out to the east on the right-hand side of the map. Zoom in a little bit more, into that area, that finger. Okay. Now if we scroll down and scroll to the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, generally speaking, what was the ethnic majority in the villages in this area of Western Srem that's south-east of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In this Srem triangle, as we call it, Lovas, Tovarnik and up to Ilok from Vukovar, the majority population was exclusively Croat. And that's why the border is so winding because when the border was drawn after the Second World War, it was drawn alongside Croat villages. If it had been straight, these Croat villages would have ended up in Serbia, in Vojvodina. That's why the boundary is so meandering because of these Croat villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you just confirm, was this the case with regard to the villages that are coloured in red, were they all ethnic majority of Croat?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you've given us a little bit about the historical significance of the oddly shaped boundaries. Can you tell us, what about the Serb population in this area? Were they originally from this Western Srem triangle, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, one smaller part is. The second part was populated, settled by Serbian population from Banja and Kordun after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could we just scroll up a little bit. I just want to -- we're missing a village in there. Okay, thank you. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you please -- just so question put in context some of your evidence, can you circle for us Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Here is Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, prior to the conflict, how many people lived in that village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: About 1700.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic makeup of that village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The greatest majority were Croats. There was only 18 -- sorry, 8 per cent of Serbs; namely, 133 residents were Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you now circle Sotin?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Sotin is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the population of Sotin?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I believe there were more Serbs in Sotin than in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many people lived in Sotin ?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Also around 1700. Perhaps around 20 per cent were Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you circle Tovarnik for us.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Tovarnik ... wait a minute. Here it is. Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the population of Tovarnik was.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Again, the majority were Croats, but there were also Serbs. I don't know exactly how many. But certainly fewer than Croats, a lot fewer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you give us a rough number of the total people -- number of people who lived in Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: About 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now could you circle for us Bapska?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Bapska is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the population in Bapska.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Bapska was exclusively Croat, in terms of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And roughly how many people lived there?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Again, around 1700, the same as in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, could you circle Ilok.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Ilok is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the population in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Again, it was a predominantly Croat population. There were some Slovaks, more Slovaks than Serbs. Serbs were in a significantly smaller number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the total population in Ilok before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Around 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to May 1991 - I want to return to Lovas, where you lived - prior to May 1991, how were the relations between the Croats and the Serbs in your village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Before and in the course of 1990 before the war escalated, the relations between Serbs and Croats were very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many police officers were assigned to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Lovas did not have a police station of its own. There were a few policemen from Lovas who worked in police stations in Vukovar and Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's clarify your last answer. You said there were a few policemen from Lovas -- I understand, okay. So the police officers who came to Lovas, where was their station?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In Tovarnik and in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you said there were a few police officers who were assigned to Lovas. What were their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in 1991, they were mainly Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness already answered that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't see where he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I -- my question is: You said there were three police officers or a few police officers who came to Lovas regularly to patrol or to perform duties in Lovas. And my question to you is: Those few police officers, what were their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted -- Mr. Witness, just one moment. Where did the witness -- or when did the witness say that there were police officers assigned to Lovas? I must have missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I look at page 10, line 11 says: There were a few policemen from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, there were a few policemen from -- from. And I think the next line is a question. It's not an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then I'll clarify. I thought it was clarified but let me clarify that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us how many police officers were assigned to Lovas; in other words, they performed duties in Lovas prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It all depends on whether you mean 1991 or before 1991. I understood we were talking about the period before 1991. At that time, police came from Tovarnik to Lovas on patrol, mainly two policemen. In the earlier years, one was Muslim and one was Serb. They came from Tovarnik. Later on, two Serbs would come, one called Rudic, a native of Lovas, and another one from Tovarnik. Before the war, they would do police work in Lovas. Before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And now can you tell us: In 1991, did that change?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In 1991, with the establishment of the Croatian state, things did change. There was a police station in Tovarnik, and, at that time, from Lovas, there were a few policemen who went to work to Tovarnik and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about in Lovas itself? Did the number of police officers who would come to Lovas to perform duties, did that change in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that changed. Croats would mainly come, but also Mica Devcic, for instance, was a Serb, a native of Lovas, who worked in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you give us roughly in this period of 1991 - obviously before October - how many police officers would be assigned to Lovas itself?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, policemen did not work in Lovas. The station was in Tovarnik, and they would come to Lovas from Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you aware of an armed skirmish that occurred on the 2nd of May, 1991, in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I know about that very well. That's when 13 policemen got killed, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt before we go on. I'm still confused about this police coming to Lovas. We know that there was no police station there. Could you get the witness do expand on how this worked in terms of policemen coming to Lovas if there was no police station? I mean, they passed through or what? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, did you understand the Judge's question? Could you answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. Police officers who were employed by the police worked at the police station in Tovarnik. They lived in Lovas and they went to work in Tovarnik. And they would come to Lovas only if required, just like things worked before 1991, as I explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the -- if required, on average, say, in a month, how many times would the police officers then have to come to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same as earlier. They would come on a weekly basis, collect information, see if there were any problems, any situations, any incidents, and then decisions would be made. But they would come once a week, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rendulic. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted just one -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Prosecutor. Sorry. Witness, we're still on this story about policemen. On page 12 of the transcript, you said there were two police officers, of which one was Serb and the other was a Muslim. These two used to come to Lovas. And later, also two policemen came, and they were Serb. And yet later, we have two Croat policemen. Was there a particular reason for the ethnic composition of the team of police who would come to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said we had to distinguish between 1991 and the period before. These policemen, Serbs, came before 1991. With the establishment of the Croatian state, things changed. And also there was no police station in Lovas. The police came from Tovarnik as required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It's clear now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Now you've testified that you're familiar with the incident on the 2nd of May, 1991 in Borovo Selo and we have evidence already before this Trial Chamber about that incident. But can you tell us what effect did this event have on the citizens of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It had a negative effect on people in Lovas and around it. Thirteen police officers, Croats, were killed, and obviously this created some tensions, problems, nervousness, among the villagers. And the situation became a bit more complicated as of then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did any of the Serbs in Lovas around this time leave Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, nobody left Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about before May? Did any of the Serbs from Lovas leave?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Young men left Lovas. I asked their parents where they went, and their interpretation was that they had gone to Vojvodina to look for work. Later on, it turned out that they were not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were these young Serb men under any pressure by the Croat population to leave Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. There were no pressures put on anybody in Lovas, including Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you've testified that later on it turned out that they were not telling the truth. What did you find out later on?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: When I went to Sid to negotiate, I found them as members of the paramilitary formations in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at some point in 1991, was a Crisis Committee formed in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. After the events in Borovo Selo, after the Croatian police officers were killed, Crisis Staffs were formed everywhere in several villages, including Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you provide us with the names of some of the members of the Crisis Committee, if you can recall them?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I can't remember all of them, but Jozo Milas was its president. Then Djuka Pilic. I myself was a member. Ivo Madzarevic was another one. There was some ten or so people. Zeljko Cirba was one of them. I can't remember all of their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. Can you tell us, when did you become a member of this Crisis Committee?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I became a member sometime in the month of July. I was recruited to join the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this Crisis Committee, or Crisis Staff, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The purpose was to monitor the developments in the village and in the other villages as well, to maintain contacts, because the situation was compounded by the developments in Borovo Selo, and the situation didn't bode well for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were the meetings of the Crisis Staff public?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were mostly public. Everybody could attend. Even some Serbs attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what measures did the Crisis Staff implement to increase security in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, we mostly worked on contacts and communication with the people in the village, with the Serbs. That's why we held meetings with the Serbs, in order to agree on the ways to maintain the integrity and the life as it was before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were check-points established around Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. After all the unfortunate events, check-points were set up at perhaps seven or eight places around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us the period during which these check-points existed, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime in June, or perhaps July, that's when they were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for how long did they exist for?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They existed until up to the 29th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have the date 29th of November, 1991. Can you confirm that that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that I -- that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: When did you leave Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I left Lovas on the 10th of October, which was the day when the attack on Lovas was mounted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did -- were these check-points still in existence when you left in October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. I said that they stopped existing on the 29th of September, which means that they were not in existence in the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We just had to clarify that for the record because the record reflected the month of November. Now, can you tell us who manned these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Those check-points were manned by Croats. They were the majority, but Serbs also did so. They were not on duty. They would often come to the check-points. Sometimes they would even bring drinks to the guys who regularly manned those check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were the men who manned these check-points, were they members of any armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, there were no armed forces in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were any of these persons from outside of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any military formations outside of Lovas and that they belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, let me rephrase my question. These men who manned the check-points in Lovas, were they from Lovas itself, or did they come from outside of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They were our local guys from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what were the duties of these men who manned these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: One of their duties was to control who was coming to the village and leaving it, to see what was going on. Because there were already groups around the village who were on reconnaissance duty. My father was approached by some troops who asked him what was going on in the village. They asked him where the Serbian cemetery was, and my father answered, There is no separate Serbian cemetery. So the main task was to be vigilant, to make sure that no incidents happened because the atmosphere was already boiling at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned their duty was to control who was coming and going from the village. Were they stopping people and preventing people from leaving or entering the village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was nothing like customs control, for example. It was just a kind of visual inspection, to see what was going on around the village. Nobody was stopped or searched or controlled in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how were these men who armed the -- the men who manned the check-point, how were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They were on guard during the night. During the day, there was no need for that because everybody could see everything. It happened during the night, and they mostly carried hunting rifles. Those men who manned the check-points during the night were given those arms by our local hunters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, during the existence of these check-points, were the weapons ever fired? Were these hunting rifles ever fired?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. Fire was never opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how did the local Serbs react to these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing. We did everything with prior consultations with them. They were happy that there were those check-points. They did not want incidents to happen on any of the sides. They did not want any problem to come from the outside. And they were happy. They were satisfied. We talked to them a lot. I myself talked to them a lot. They never expressed satisfaction [as interpreted], at least those Serbs, those locals of Lovas that we lived with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The record says that you stated: "They never expressed satisfaction." Can you clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: What I meant was that there was dissatisfaction but for some other reasons. But when it comes to people trying to maintain order in the village, they were satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was the Crisis Committee involved in the creation of any armed formations in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. As I've already told you, there were no armed formations in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did the Crisis Committee acquire any explosives?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did not acquire any explosives, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was there a point in time when Lovas received some mines from somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, yes. Those were anti-armour mines, anti-tank mines, that were delivered from Ilok and they were returned to Ilok in late September. Those mines were from Ilok. We didn't want to use them. They remained at the depot, and they were returned to Ilok on the 29th of September. And they came from Ilok, because, at one point in time, there was a lot of military activity going on around Ilok, including JNA tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many anti-tank mines were received?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Some 15 or so, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why weren't they used? Why weren't they planted anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They were not planted because the village functioned normally. People would go into the fields with tractors to farm the land, and that's why we thought that it would have been more of a problem if we had planted those mines than if we hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, did the Crisis Staff take any actions to dispel any concerns of the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I've already told you, I talked a lot with the Serbs. We had a meeting in Mirko Lovric's house. He was a Serb. And they themselves gathered and invited us to come, and it was not the other way around. We did not want to always invite them. We didn't want those initiatives always to come from us. We told them, Okay, whenever you want, you gather wherever you want and invite us and we'll come and talk to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when this meeting at Mr. Lovric's house occurred?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was immediately after the incident in Borovo. The end of May or perhaps the beginning of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sometime in July 1991, do you recall an incident involving the JNA at the Lovas co-operative?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Olmsted. There's a small point, nothing may turn on it. But before you go into another area -- Mr. Rendulic, you mentioned earlier that you had been recruited to the Crisis Staff. My question is in two parts. The first part is, does it mean you didn't volunteer; and the second part is, who recruited you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I volunteered. However, that was upon the invitation of my secretary who worked with me in my company and he was the president of the Crisis Staff, so when he asked me whether I would join, in view of the fact that I had a possibility to influence people through the farm, although I was not an HDZ member, he was of an opinion that I would make a great contribution in calming the situation down between the Croats and the Serbs, which is why he invited me to join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to my question. Sometime in July 1991, do you recall an incident involving the JNA soldiers at the Lovas co-operative?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I remember there was a minor incident. The military came. I don't know whether they were reservists or the regular JNA. They came to the farm. They removed the Croatian flag from the building. They made a guard do it. And then they forced Nikica Maric to climb a silo, which is about 22 metres high, and to remove the flag from there. Nobody wanted to do that so they forced Nikica Maric to do that. And further on, they demanded from the guard the key to a cupboard where two rifles were locked up. Those rifles belonged to the guards. Those were M-48 old rifles. The troops took the key from the guard. They took the rifles away. They promised that they would return them to us, but they never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In August 1991, did you attend a meeting with any members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were a lot of contacts with the JNA. In the month of August, the road between Tovarnik and Lovas or, rather, Sid was blocked. At that time, we still used Sid which is in Serbia. People went there for various things, for example, to buy medicines and other things. Vukovar was already encircled. So we could no go to Vukovar so we had to go to Sid. The reservists of the Novi Sad Corps blocked the road and they no longer allowed the police officers to go to Tovarnik where they worked. Myself, Djuro Prodanovic and Zeljko Cirba went to talk to the reservist in order to ask him to lift the blockade of the road to allow the free passage of our villagers and they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of the JNA officer with whom you met that day?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I -- they told us that they were reservist from the Novi Sad Corps. There was a lieutenant-colonel, a younger man, whose name I don't remember, and another one was a Major Radosavljevic who told us that he was from Sid. He knew us. He was familiar with Lovas. He often came to Lovas to do some business there, and he said that he was a familiar with a lot of people from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did this JNA major tell you -- tell the Lovas delegation anything, as far as information he had about Lovas and Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He told us at the place where we were that he knew Lovas, that he knew people, that it was a peaceful village, that there were no problems in that village. He told us that they -- they had been sent from the Novi Sad Corps with an instruction, according to which that there were 2.000 Ustasha there, and that was not true, which they finally realised themselves. And at the end of that meeting he said, Don't touch us. We won't touch you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many armed men were there in Lovas at this time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Armed people. I don't know. If you want to take into account hunting rifles, I would say that some 35 men were armed, but the arms in question were hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Lovas, was there ever a ZNG unit in the village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Before the attack at the beginning of May, there was a group of some ten to 12 men who were ZNG. They were billeted in the old school. They were there for perhaps ten or 15 days, after which they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while they were in Lovas for this short period of time, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Nothing. They drove their cars around the village. They went to -- to Tovarnik and back. Everything was calm. Nothing was happening, and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know why they left?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know why they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now beside this is -- strike that question. Now did you give this information regarding the number of armed men in Lovas, as well as this information about this ZNG unit, to the major at this meeting regarding the blockade?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. We discussed things quite openly. He said that he knew Lovas very well. I really don't remember whether we mentioned the ZNG members. Our conversation was very open and very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Setting aside the ZNG unit that was in Lovas temporarily, did you inform the major that his information about the 2.000 Ustasha was incorrect and that there was much fewer armed men in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did he verify the information you provided him?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he verified the information. There was no need to verify anything because no information that they had was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this meeting, did it -- where did it take place? Did it take place at the blockade itself?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was actually on the road between Tovarnik and Lovas. It was in a field by that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during this meeting, did you have the opportunity to inspect any of the JNA vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, as we were talking, I told that major I have never seen a tank. And he told me, Do you want to see one? I said yes. He said, Okay. Climb the tank. And then I climbed the tank. I saw a machine-gun with live ammunition, and I said, Well, now I'm looking at a tank but this is live ammunition. And even if it is, the most important thing is that we -- you don't open fire. And then one of the soldiers who was sitting on the tank said, Why shouldn't we be opening fire on you Ustasha? And then the major said, You can't say that they are Ustasha. They are from Lovas. They are people who are good. And then that reservist attacked the major. He told him, Why did you allow the police and those Ustasha to go to Tovarnik and I have to be on duty here? I realised that the situation was not that good, and I went back to my group with Cirba and the others. And the lieutenant-colonel who was there, he says, He is a member of the Territorial Defence. He is a bit exclusive in what he says and what he does, but we will see to him so you don't have to be concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that the JNA lifted the blockade. When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, it happened as we were talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to turn to another topic now. Were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Witness, you -- you told us that, more or less, 30 to 35 people in Lovas had hunting rifles; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So meaning that they were hunters. Now my question is: At that time, did you consider them as armed men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We considered them to be civilians who were only using hunting rifles given to them by our local hunters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question -- my question, in fact, is: The local hunters, you -- you would not consider them to be armed men, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, we didn't. It's sports organisation. A sports association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, if I may just clarify a little bit further Judge Delvoie's question. These 30 men, are you referring to the men who are manning these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Those were men not on the barricades but men who stood guard around the village. We did not have any barricades around our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't use the word "barricades." I meant the check-points. You've mentioned that there were seven or so check-points around --

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the men who manned the check-points. But overnight, for them to feel safer not completely without weapons, huntsmen lent their weapons to other people. I, for instance, was at a check-point, and when I left, I handed over my weapon to another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now I want to move onto another topic. Were you in Sotin on the 28th [Realtime transcript read in error "22nd"] of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of August, I was in Sotin. I went to Sotin quite often because my half-brother and his family lived there. So I was there often. I was there on the 22nd but also on the 26th when my nephew got killed in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps I misspoke. I meant to say the 28th of August. I want to talk about events on the 28th of August in Sotin.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, I was there for the funeral of my nephew who got killed in Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many people attended that funeral?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: More than 100. Between 100 and 150 people, both from Lovas and from Sotin. My brother was from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any women and children at the funeral?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Very many. Women and children too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened during the course of that funeral that day.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: When the religious rites were performed in the yard of the house where my nephew had lived, we walked from the yard up to a small park and then two planes arrived, planes of the Galeb type, and we thought they were flying to Vukovar because Vukovar was under a blockade since 19 -- since the 28th. Somebody said, Watch out, planes. And then the whole procession scattered while my daughter and I just threw ourselves on the ground and that's when the planes started firing from machine-guns. One of the planes took a U-turn and dropped a bomb just outside the house of my nephew. Our good fortune was that we had started with the funeral 15 minutes earlier than scheduled. The funeral was scheduled for 1600 hours, and we listened to the priest and started earlier because exactly at a quarter past 4.00 p.m. that bomb was dropped outside the house of my nephew, and if we had still been there, as planned before, it would have killed a lot of people, hundreds of people. And when we returned finally, we found the -- the fence and the walls bullet ridden.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you able to determine who the planes belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We knew that. Those were JNA planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you suspect that the Serbs in Sotin played any role in this attack; and, if so, why you believed that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We believed so. Because it was widely known that funeral was scheduled for 4.00 p.m. so somebody must have told them about it. And they treated it as an Ustasha funeral. It was even said that we had to watch out because there would be an attack on Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, after this attack on the funeral, what happened later that night in Sotin?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that funeral could not take place until that evening. They took the body of my nephew to the cemetery by night. The next morning, one or two armoured vehicles entered and started firing from heavy machine-guns at the houses in Sotin. And during that night, one busload of Sotin residents fled to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in the days that followed this attack, did you have opportunity to see any of the destruction in Sotin?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. The very next morning, I went to Sotin, taking my sister-in-law and her colleagues to take their things because they had fled to Lovas the night before, and then I could see houses striped with bullets and holes in facades and many shattered windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the population in Sotin offer any armed resistance to this attack?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. There was no resistance certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that a busload of Croat civilians from -- or citizens from Sotin came to Lovas. Roughly how many were in there bus?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: About 50 people. It was that double bus driven by Boro from the Vupik company. He drove that bus. Some 50, 60 people fled in that bus, whereas some arrived in their own cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these Sotin citizens who arrived in Lovas, were they carrying any weapons or wearing any military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, certainly not. Those were civilians, including women and children, who went the next day via Lipovac to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, after the night of the 28th/29th of August, was Sotin attacked again?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was the night of the 28th, and after that, I think there were no more attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about after Lovas was attacked? Was Sotin ever attacked again?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Sotin was attacked later, after Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the nature of that attack?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The usual kind. First of all, an attack by JNA artillery; then the military troops would -- came in. The pattern was the same, for Bapska, Sotin and Lovas. Artillery first followed by infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move into September of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Witness, you said that the funeral was considered -- the funeral of your nephew was considered an Ustasha funeral. Why was that? Had that anything to do with what your nephew was doing when killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me try to make it clearer. The boy went with a group after being called up. The report was that Chetniks had occupied an important building in Borovo. Those who were then in Vukovar went to liberate that building, and when their group arrived, the paramilitary forces and the Chetniks were already inside the building. The hall of engineers it was called. And as they were approaching the hall of engineers, one Zolja hand-held rocket was fired. It hit the wall. A piece of the wall hit my nephew. He was the last in the group to enter the building. The others could not be hurt. And then they saw a Chetnik hit the boy on the head, almost took his scalp off. That's what we were told later when he arrived at the hospital. So from Borovo village, those paramilitaries and Territorial Defence members raided the village, and in comparison with those paramilitary forces, he was treated as an Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify your last answer, was your nephew a member of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, no. They were also civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what organisation he was with? Was it the local TO?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. The local one, just as in Lovas. There were those territorial guards. They were called in to help, to get those Chetniks out of the hall of engineers in Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move to September 1991. What happened in Tovarnik that month?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In September 1991 is the month where a holiday is celebrated in Tovarnik, a patron saint of the church. That's when the JNA and paramilitary forces attacked Tovarnik according to the same pattern: First an artillery attack, followed by a raid by infantry. Most of the population fled to Lovas and, of course, they said there were a lot of casualties. Towers on the churches were also destroyed, and many buildings were damaged, and half of them practically came to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you give us the approximate date of this attack?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 22nd. It was Saint Matthew's. That's the church holiday in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there any ZNG or other Croat armed forces in Tovarnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. There was just the Croatian police and there were no armed units whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did the Croat population in Tovarnik offer any armed resistance to this attack?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, there was no armed resistance because everybody fled to Lovas, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And those who fled to Lovas, were they wearing any military uniforms or carrying any arms?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No way. Those were mainly civilians. From what I saw in my street and in my village, and the people who came to the Crisis Staff, all of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to witness the destruction in Tovarnik first-hand?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to see that when I went to Sid for negotiations on the 27th and the 28th. Negotiations with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Given the level of destruction that you observed in Tovarnik, were you able to conclude who engaged in that attack?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was not my conclusion. I saw who was there. Because when we travelled to Sid for those negotiations on the 27th September, in the afternoon, we were led by a JNA officer and we saw there a lot of JNA troops and paramilitary units. From Tovarnik until outside Sid, there were a lot of vehicles, armoured vehicles, tanks and trucks, and we saw a lot of troops. It was a warm summer day. They were standing outside their vehicles. Some were even shaving in the field. Apart from the JNA, there were paramilitary forces, many disheveled men with long beards, something that would not tolerated in the JNA. There was a lot of destruction around, transmission lines brought down, a lot of dead cattle. The towers on the Catholic church burned down. But the main impression was the great numbers of JNA troops and paramilitary unit members. Everything almost -- everything in sight was full of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you see any houses in Tovarnik destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I told you, I saw many burnt-down and destroyed houses. The roofs had burnt, and you could see holes from shells, and there were no more towers on the churches, and one church was still burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what were the circumstances that brought you to Tovarnik on that date?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We came because the priest, late Ivan Burik, had come to Lovas to see our parish priest while I was there with a colleague to pay for the funeral service for my nephew, and he said, You have to go quickly to negotiate with the army in Tovarnik because Lovas will be attacked. The Howitzers and mortars are already in place. Lovas will be attacked tomorrow unless you come to Tovarnik to negotiate with the army. So the three of us got ready. Zeljko Cirba, Milan Tepavac, I, and we also took one Serb representative. The group of us went to Tovarnik to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Milan Tepavac?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb. I said we took a Serb representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why did a Serb attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that we in the Crisis Staff did not conceal anything. All the information was open to the Serbs too. We did not want to have any exclusively Croat groups, and we always co-opted Serb representatives for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So at the time of this meeting, were there Serbs who were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no official members but they were almost regularly invited to attend meetings of the Crisis Staff because there were no secrets. All the talk was about keeping good, peaceful relations in the village that we used to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did the meeting with the JNA ultimately take place?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We thought it would be a meeting in Tovarnik. However, when we came, outside Tovarnik at a place called Vezic [phoen], a soldier came out of an armoured vehicle. It turned out later he was Lieutenant-Colonel Savkic [as interpreted]. He brought out a blanket. We had brought some drinks. We sat down. He accepted the drinks. We talked a little. He told us some things that took us by surprise. He said, among other things, Brothers, look at what is going on. Why is so much property destroyed in Tovarnik? Why is there no reaction? How long will this last? How long will it go on? And then he said, We have no way of talking here in Tovarnik. We have to go to the command in Sid to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. And in what building in Sid did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: After the police inspection in Tovarnik, we had to go on. We had no [indiscernible]. Then the officer didn't know who we were. We couldn't get passes, and then we ended up in the schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from what you could observe at the schoolhouse in Sid, what was based there?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In Sid, we also saw a lot of troops at the fair-grounds, a high concentration of military vehicles and troops, a lot of soldiers also around the school. Sid was crawling with army troops, JNA and I don't know who else. We went into a classroom in that school, and we were met by JNA officers. We thought those would be talks around a table. However, we had to sit down in places where students sit, whereas they sat on the other side and started questioning us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now before we get to the substance of this meeting, on the road from Tovarnik to Sid, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I've said already we saw a lot of troops and a large number of military vehicles, tanks and trucks, and many troops were outside their vehicles. It was a very nice day. They were standing along the road. From Tovarnik all the way up to Sid, you could see large columns. The area around the road was completely green from those vehicles and troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, do you recall who from the JNA was present at this meeting at the school in Sid?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Those were all high-ranking officers. One of them, Zelimir Petrovic talked most of the time. He was from KOS, the military intelligence service. That's how he introduced himself. There was also an older man, Milic Jovic. And the rest were majors, JNA majors who kept records, took notes, and were mainly observers of the questioning led by Zelimir Petrovic, a member of the KOS, which is the counter-intelligence service from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during this meeting, did the JNA officers make any claims about the number of weapons in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They, too, had the same kind of reports we heard about when we met with the Novi Sad Corps. This one was also from Novi Sad Corps. They had reports that there were many armed men in Lovas, many Ustashas, that kind of report. Although they had very precise information what exactly is going on in Lovas, we said that was not true. We said we have this, this, and that. The situation is calm. There are no problems, and what they are telling us is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that these JNA officers already were aware of the number of weapons, the actual number of weapons, in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They do -- they -- they knew not only that. They knew everything. He -- one of them told me, Is it true that at such and such an hour on that day the lights were on at night in our school? And he told me, What was that about? And I said, A wounded person was brought on that night and we had called in Dr. Kacar, a Serb, to treat the man. So they had information that a light was on at the precise hour on a particular day. Of course, they knew everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now did the JNA officers issue any demands on the population of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of that conversation, Zelimir Petrovic said that Lovas must hand back weapons in the amount they mentioned. We said, We don't have that many. And then they said, Okay. Hand over what you have. The very next morning, a certain colonel would come together with an officer who had brought us there, and then army troops would come to collect the weapons and to check whether anything else remained in houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us the name of the officer that brought you there? I don't know if we got that on the record. JNA officer that brought you to Sid that day.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: That was Lieutenant-Colonel Radisavkic from Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did the JNA officers tell you would happen if the Lovas population did not comply with their demands?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They said, If you don't surrender the weapons, and in the event that a single bullet is fired at the army, be it in the village or in the field, they would raze Lovas to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed it is, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Witness, we'll take the first break now. We'll come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would just like to announce that the Prosecution has been joined by one of our interns, Francois Braun. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It was on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It was on. I didn't have my headphones on. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And also, I have been asked by the Registrar to say on the record that the map that I showed the witness, we're not interested in tendering that. That has already been admitted and he just circled a few villages. So that can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Rendulic. I just want to return very quickly to this meeting with the JNA on the 27th of September. After the JNA officers issued these demands on the population of Lovas, what did you tell them you would do with those demands?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We told them that what they were asking us to do is impossible to comply with. That we didn't have those weapons, that we would talk to the locals, that we would have a meeting that same evening, and that he -- that we would convey the message given to us by them in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, hold that meeting in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That same evening, when we returned, we held the meeting with the locals. We told them what the situation was like. I told them whey saw in Tovarnik and in Sid. A lot of troops, namely. I told them that we had to endeavour to keep peace to avoid any conflict, that we should endeavour for all the weapons to be surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how did the Lovas population respond to this information?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, their reactions differed. Most of them were afraid as to what would happen because they were told that the troops would arrive in the village the following morning. They knew what had happened in Tovarnik when the JNA and paramilitaries entered, that there were a lot of dead and wounded people and destroyed houses. Of course, people were afraid, and during the night a lot of them left and went to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what were the age groups and genders that left that night?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Women and children, including my own wife and children. Mostly civilians who went to Tovarnik that night. They were afraid. They feared the arrival of the JNA and paramilitaries. That's why almost half the village left that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did anyone in Lovas turn in their weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: A certain number of people did bring the weapons. Three Kalashnikovs and the rest were hunting rifles and pistols. Obviously those pistols belonged to the hunters who had licences to carry them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you give us roughly a number of fire-arms that were turned in?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: All in all, up to 20 pieces were handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why were some of the fire-arms kept by people?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, some kept the weapons. They didn't want to hand them over. They said, This belongs to me. I paid for it. If the army wants to take it away from me, they can come and take it away themselves. Because the military was aware of who had weapons. All of those weapons were licensed by the police, so it was not a problem at all to know who had weapons, because all of those weapons were purchased against licences issued by the police, as sports weapons and hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about offering armed resistance to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, nobody mentioned that. After what we saw in Tovarnik, I and others said that we really could not resist anybody, that nothing should be done, that the JNA and the paramilitary units should not be provoked at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what happened the next day, on the 28th of September?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of September, in the morning, Priest Burik came from Tovarnik together with that same officer, Radisavkic. We had a brief conversation there. We showed them the weapons that we had collected, and then the officer said that that was not enough, that that's not what we had discussed, that we had to come back to Sid for another round of talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who from Lovas went for that second round of talks?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Again, myself, a Lieutenant-Colonel Antun Lovric, Franjo Krizmanic and a representative of the Serbs, Milan Tepavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned a Lieutenant-Colonel Antun Lovric. Was he an active member of any unit?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. He was actually a retired colonel of the JNA who resided in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was this second meeting at the same location in Sid?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the way, we stopped by in Tovarnik where we talked to some former residents of Lovas who were Serbs and who were members of paramilitary formations. And then we went to the elementary school to talk to Zelimir Petrovic that time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that on the way to Sid that day you encountered some Serbs who were from Lovas. Could you tell us the names of those Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, in the police station that they allegedly ran, there was Zeljko Krnjaic, a man called Grkovic, and there were some other men unknown to me. And on the road, I bumped into Milan Devcic. I have already told you that he had been a Croatian police officer. And we were discussing the situation in Lovas. Those in front of the police station and Vorkapic was there, Grkovic was with them, as well as Krnjaic who was allegedly the head of that police station in Tovarnik. They told me, Aco, which is my nickname, Aco, make sure that nothing happens in Lovas because we will raze it to the ground. I told them, Nothing happened so far, nothing will probably happen in the future. I bumped into Milan Devcic on the road and he asked me, Aco, where is my father? I said, I saw him a half an hour ago. He drove through the village on his motorbike. He also told me, Make sure that nothing happens in the village. And my answer was the same: Nothing has happened so far and we will make sure that, on our side, nothing happens in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, you mentioned that Krnjaic was head of a police station. What station was that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was the newly established police station, the one that was established after the fall of Tovarnik. Either the JNA or the Serbian paramilitary formations set it up in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to now go to this meeting, this second meeting in Sid. You mentioned that Colonel Petrovic was there. What did you tell Colonel Petrovic about the situation in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We told him that we had held that meeting the day before in Lovas. We explained to everybody what was requested from us, and that it was impossible to fulfil those requests because we did not have that many weapons. We said that half the population had fled to Ilok during the night and they asked us why they had fled. I told them that after having seen what was going on in Tovarnik, the killings, the setting houses on fire, people were afraid and they fled to Ilok during the night. And then he responded that he had just arrived from Belgrade, from the KOS organisation, as a KOS colonel, and he was supposed to place paramilitaries under the JNA control to curb the crimes because that is not what the JNA did. That's why he had been sent to put those paramilitaries under the control of JNA units in order to stop their wilful behaviour. That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please instruct the witness to slow down a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters are asking whether you could speak a little bit more slowly so that they can follow. And I have a question of you about your meeting, the previous one. What exactly was requested from you? From Lovas, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To surrender the weapons that we had, to hand it over to the military on the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On the second meeting, you -- you told the JNA officer that you couldn't meet their requirements. Was there a quotum? Did you have to give them a certain amount of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They said that we had a lot of weaponry, that there were as many as 2.000 soldiers who had a lot of weapons. And that was not correct. We told them that we probably had up to 35 pieces of mostly hunting rifles. That that's all that we could hand over, that we could not meet their request because it was simply unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So their request would have been, then, the weapons of about 2.000 men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose so. But, in practical terms, it was not possible. Because we told them that the number was nearly -- not nearly as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that Colonel Petrovic was with an organisation called KOS. I don't know if we've heard that before. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It's the counter-intelligence service of the then-JNA. To be honest, I really don't know what that service did, what its main task was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During this meeting with Colonel Petrovic, did you tell him anything about how the Serb population was being treated in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, I told him that in Lovas nothing extraordinary was happening, no pressure was put on the Serbian population, the Serbian population was not provoked. I told him that everything had been calm and in good order up to then. And then I asked him, Colonel, what is this? How long is this going to go on for? And he told me, For as long as the people told us, whether what Milosevic and Tudjman were plotting was, indeed, what we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was Milan Tepavac at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milan was with us during the first and the second meetings. He mostly kept quiet. He did not say much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you were talking about how the Serbs were being treated in Lovas, did he disagree with your assessment?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, no. He basically, if anything, he supported our words. He supported us in what we were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now what did Colonel Petrovic instruct the Lovas delegation to do with regard to weapons at that point, at that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: At that second meeting, he said the army never even wanted their weapons that had been handed over. He told us to try and persuade the population to return from Ilok to Lovas. And later Father Burik asked, What about Tovarnik? And Petrovic told him the same, Try and persuade the population to come back, those people from Tovarnik who had fled. And when the population eventually returned, and when the weapons were collected in Lovas, they would come to verify the situation and may it -- and that they would make sure that all the weapons had, indeed, been handed over. However, they never reappeared in Lovas after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So they never came to conduct those searches for weapons.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, they never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did -- they never collected the weapons that you had managed to gather from the Lovas population?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, never. They never came to pick up the weapons that had been collected previously or to check whether more was collected after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did Colonel Petrovic issue any additional warnings at this second meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Save for what I have already told you about the return of the population and about collecting weapons, nothing. When we got out of the house, he told the troops, These men did not do what we had agreed yesterday, so there's no need for us to go to Lovas today. The troops were already line -- lined up ready to search the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What happened to -- you mentioned the late priest Burik. What happened to him after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He returned to Tovarnik, and after the fall of Lovas on the 10th of October, when paramilitaries stormed Lovas, some seven or eight days later, he was killed in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was his body ever found?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. His body was found. It was exhumed and eventually buried in the Tovarnik cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did the Lovas delegation do when it returned from this second meeting to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We told the locals that the military would not come to the village at that point in time but that didn't mean that they would never come. Petrovic told us that no fire should be opened on the military because if one single bullet was fired, they would raze Lovas to the ground. During the second meeting, when we spoke to Petrovic, we told him that we could not be held responsible for what was -- what was happening outside of the village in the field, that we can only guarantee the security situation and the safety of the military in the village itself, in Lovas, not outside of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what happened on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, there was the first attack on Lovas. Not Lovas itself but on the perimeter of our company, including silos. The JNA that had been stationed in the Sid forest in Serbia arrived with tanks close to the silos, some 3 kilometres away, and around 11.00 that morning, tanks opened fire on our silos. I was in my office, together with my colleagues. We heard explosions. We thought that the centre of village was targeted, but it was not the centre of village but the perimeter of the company and the silos. Some ten shells all together were fired on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware of any reasons why the JNA would shell the Lovas agricultural co-op?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: After all the talks, after all the negotiations with the army in Sid, and based on their behaviour, there was really no reason whatsoever for their attack on our facilities in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were any Croat houses destroyed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
