utterances.text: Only one belonging to Tadija Bekcevic, who was our employee. That was the only house that was hit on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened on the 3rd of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of October, there was another attack. I sent out men to collect the grains that spilled out from the silos. And we had a warehouse with apples. The roof was destroyed. I sent my men out to protect the apples and to collect the grains from the silos. And I went to Ilok. When I returned, I bumped into a villager and he told me that there was another attack. A tank attack from the same direction, from the direction of Sid, and, again, the main target was our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now can you tell us what happened on the 5th of October in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of October, there was an attack on the village, i.e., on our church, and the church tower was set on fire by Maljutka shells that were fired from tanks. And those Maljutkas set the church tower on fire on the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any armed units in that church?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now during this period that we've been discussing - let's call it the -- between 28 September through the 5th or 6th of October - did any of the Croat population who had left Lovas return to it?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Between the 5th and the 10th October, there was a -- a period of calm of sorts. Nothing was happening. Some people went to Ilok; some returned. They had cattle in Lovas. That's why they returned, to feed the cattle. So there was a lot of movement between Ilok and Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And now if you could tell us what happened on the morning of the 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In the morning on the 10th of October, there was an attack on Lovas. It started with an artillery attack, by tank shelling and mortar fire which was opened on the part of the village that belonged exclusively to Croats. There were no Serb houses there. This is the eastern area in the direction of cemetery. My house, which is a one-storey house, was what they targeted, and some six or seven shells fell around my house. It was prominent, and they set their aims around my house which was in the Croatian part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to this attack on the 10th of October, did the JNA or anyone else issue any warnings that an attack was imminent?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, nobody said anything. There were no warnings, announcements of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned around six shells fell in the immediate vicinity of your house. Can you tell us, if you can, the total number of shells that you recall falling that day?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I know what happened around my house. In subsequent conversations, I learned that some 15 to 20 shells - not more than that - fell on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen 65 ter 2961. This is tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, what we have in front of us is a map of Lovas. You mentioned that the shelling occurred in an area that was exclusively Croat. Could you circle on this map that area that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: You can see the church in the eastern part of the village. And my street is very close to the cemetery. This is the part of the village where the shells fell on that day. Nothing happened in the north-western part of the village because there were some Serbian houses there. In this part here, however, there were no Serbian houses at all, and this is where the shells mostly fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in that area, were there any military installations or factories?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, no. There were no factories or anything. This is a residential area with civilian properties. There were no military there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you mark - maybe draw an arrow - from the direction from which the shells came?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Those shells came from the southern part of the region, from the Sid-Tovarnik road, or from what we knew as Jelas forest. This is where you enter the village and this is the road leading towards Tovarnik and from that direction, the shells came.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you mark that arrow with an A so we can identify it later.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the attack started with artillery. What followed the attack by artillery?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The artillery attack -- the situation became calm for a while. We started talking. My neighbour with two young children came to my house. We spent some time in the cellar, and then they we went to the house of my parents-in-law, who were in the cellar in that house. And then, while we were in that cellar, we heard infantry fire, both bursts of fire and individual shots, and all of a sudden -- actually we thought that it was close to our house but, no, those were dum-dum bullets that exploded with a lot of noise. I was afraid that those paramilitary units reached our own houses. However, they set out from the north-western part, the same area where I already drew an arrow. We thought that they would come from Sid, but, no, they came from the direction of Vukovar, from the north-west of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see that you created a arrow indicating the direction in which the armed forces entered Lovas. Could you mark that with a B.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P314. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, were any Croat homes seriously damaged during the shelling part of the attack on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was damage. What I saw in my part of the street is that the house across from me was hit, killing a certain gentleman, Milan Latas, who was a Serb. To the left of his house, again facing mine, the house was completely destroyed because it was hit directly. On my side of the street, the house of my father-in-law next door was hit by a shell, which wounded a woman, and another shell hit my father-in-law's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after the shelling occurred and the armed units entered your neighbourhood, were additional homes destroyed; and, if so, can you tell us how many?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: As I said, the shelling was around 7.20. That was damage done by shells. And when the paramilitary units entered the village, other houses were damaged by infantry fire. Soldiers went from one house to another down the street, and it must have been some sort of system for them. These paramilitary units were led by Serbs, burning houses down, and that's how my house was burnt down too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How many houses were burnt down that day; if you know?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: About 20 to 30 houses. I can't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, how many Croats were killed during this attack?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: That first day, we got a report from the European observers that 21 Croats were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the European observers go to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. From Ilok, they went to Lovas. We had told them about the situation and they went. I was supposed to go with them. However, they could not guarantee my safety there, so I did not accompany them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 5062 on the screen. This is tab 29. And I ask that this not be broadcast because it's protected. Now what we have in front of us is a report dated 18 October 1991. And if we could turn to page 3 of the original. For the translation, I'm interested in 03041190.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This document lists 22 Croat civilians. Can you confirm, were these among the individuals that were killed on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. These people were killed on the 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you see the corpses or the corpse of any of these persons on this list?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I saw one body when I was fleeing from my yard. There was one body. I later found out it was the body of Zivan Antolovic, who lived not far for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And all right. For the record we see that name under number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P315, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. That's correct, it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, did the Croat population in Lovas offer any armed resistance during the attack on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, there was no resistance whatsoever. Because, as I said, from the north-west, there were refugees, Serbs, displaced people, and from the other side, there was no opportunity to offer any resistance. There were no weapons. Nobody. We, from that side of the village, also fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you had the opportunity to observe some of the Serb armed units that came into Lovas that day. Can you tell us, what kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: All sorts. There were military uniforms, camouflage uniforms, and pieces of civilian clothing. For instance, blue workers' overalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that they were obviously shooting their weapons but in addition burning some of the houses. Did you hear them saying anything when they were in your area?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I overheard a lot. When they came to my house, luckily they passed by my father-in-law's house where I was in the basement with my in-laws and two girls. It's just 10 metres away from my house. I heard them open the door of my garage, enter my house. I heard them shouting, He's not at home. The car is gone. And one of them said, He is an HDZ man. And a neighbour of mine, Kata Gordic [as interpreted], who overheard it said, trying to mollify them, No, he is not HDZ. He is a Communist. And another one of them said, Milan, look at this, look at that. It was a Lika cap, at least I supposed so. I heard one of the paramilitary men wore a Lika cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that you left Lovas. Did you leave Lovas on that day of that attack, after you made these observations?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day I left around 12.00. My in-laws and that woman with two children said they were going to surrender. I said, I'm not going to surrender, I'm staying in the basement. However, a few minutes later, that neighbour woman came and said, Aca, look, your house is burning. And before that, I heard two explosions. They had some phosphate bombs that would turn the house into a blaze in a second. Instinctively, I ran out of the basement and I saw my house burning. I saw the curtains burning upstairs, and smoke was billowing from the door. Then somebody said to me, Aco, let's go into the yard. You have this 10-metre-long yard that leads to the backyard, and when we got there I entered the stable and I heard at that moment the paramilitaries open the door between me and the backyard, shouting, Is there anyone in the basement? Get out. And at that moment, I told my in-laws and that woman, I am going to make a run for it. And I did. And I ran eventually into a house that was at the end of the village. I looked back and my entire house was in flames by that time. From that cornfield, I ran on until I met up with some other people who had fled on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did you end up that day?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: That day, we talked, trying to decide what to do. Some people said they would stay in huts on the periphery. I said it made no sense, we should go to Ilok. So a group of us went towards Mohovo. In Mohovo we stayed in a local office where we found some more of Lovas residents who had fled. And that evening, Marin Balic from Mohovo and another man from my village went to Ilok and told them in Ilok what had happened. Whereas most of us from Lovas remained in Mohovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rendulic. But given our time, I will ask you to just try to keep your answers a little bit shorter. While you were in Mohovo, did you learn which Serb forces had entered Lovas that day?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I found out that it was the Vorkapics and Krnjaics we discussed before who came with the paramilitaries. In fact, it was not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who led this group, this paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: That paramilitary group, as we heard from Lisac who led them, the Croat who had been captured in Tovarnik, was led by our local resident, a Serb, Milan [as interpreted] Devetak. And that group had about 180 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after you were in Mohovo, where did you go to? What village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I see here it says Milan Devetak I said, in fact, Ljuban. Ljuban Devetak was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. After you were in Mohovo, what village did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: After Mohovo we went to town, to Ilok. Overnight, those two friends of mine and I went to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Ilok, what was the situation in that village at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: You mean in the town of Ilok? The situation there was rather turbulent too. People already knew what was going on in Tovarnik. Many people had come from Ilaca that was attacked, Tovarnik as well, and from Bapska. There had been an artillery attack in Bapska and the situation was very volatile.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many refugees were in Ilok at this time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I think there were 6.000 or so residents and about 6.000 refugees from the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were these refugees Croats?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why -- why Ilok? Why were they all coming to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: That was the only place it was possible to go. Vukovar was under siege. The area on the -- in the south was also controlled by military units. The only place you could go was Ilok. Ilok is a place on the Danube river and you couldn't go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while you were in Ilok, were you able to observe any of the JNA forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, we saw a large concentration of JNA forces, including armoured vehicles, machine-gun nests around Ilok. Because a good part of Ilok is in a depression, surrounded by elevations, so you could see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you see any artillery cannons or anything like that around the area?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We saw mortars, machine-gun nests, armoured vehicles on the road overlooking Ilok, and that was the road from Backa Palanka to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in which direction were their weapons aimed?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: All the weapons were trained at the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Now you've testified that you arrived Ilok on the 10th of October. Can you tell us what happened on the morning of the 11th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 11th, I was invited by the residents of Ilok, by Petar Cobankovic to come there, and join them for negotiations with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you know what position Mr. Cobankovic held at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He was president of the Crisis Staff in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did he tell you why they were inviting you to the meeting with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They invited me to come and describe what had happened the day before in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did Mr. Cobankovic explain to you the situation with the JNA in Ilok up to that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was calm in Ilok, except for the fact that the JNA encircled Ilok from the eastern side, and it was very difficult with the number of people in Ilok. The mill was operating, and there was still power at the time when the refugees came, but later on, the power supply was cut off from Palanka, so the situation became more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, prior to the meeting with the JNA on the 11th of October, did you learning anything about what had happened in Bapska?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The people from Bapska said that they had also suffered an artillery attack on the 5th of October, I believe, and on that occasion, one of my friends, veterinarian Josip, was wounded and later succumbed to that wound. Josip Vulic is the name, I now remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 418 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Rendulic, the report we have in front of us for the moment gives a list of buried civilians killed in the battle to liberate Lovas and then a list of combatants killed in the liberation of Lovas and there is one name mentioned, Djordjevic, volunteer from Serbia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You told us no resistance was mounted in Lovas. Do you know what happened to this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no fighting in Lovas and these were not combatants. These were civilians who did not get killed. They were executed, taken away from their homes and executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Rendulic. It's not about the 22 persons in the first part of the document. It's about the next name under list of combatants, and there is a name Djordjevic which would be a volunteer from Serbia. So I presume that's somebody from the other side. So do you know what happened to him? How did he -- how did he get killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to explain this. It says: "Fighting for the liberation of Lovas." Those were not combatants. Those were civilians and I want to correct that. As for this Djordjevic who got killed in Lovas, this was the matter. The first of our natives who got out of Lovas was killed on the way to Opatovac, that's the side from which paramilitaries came. That man was hit by a bullet but he wasn't killed. He was still alive when this Djordjevic man approached him and shot him dead with a pistol while he was lying wounded. That's the explanation about this Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But this document says that this -- this Djordjevic himself got killed. Perhaps you don't know about it. Then just say so. Do you know that this man, Djordjevic, was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that one of the paramilitaries got killed just after sunrise. But the explanation we heard was that he approached the wounded man, who, while wounded, managed to kill him by shooting his pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. Picking up on the question from the President, we are still on the day of the 10th of October. You said on that day, if I understood you correctly, that the attack on Lovas began with an artillery attack, followed by fire from tanks and mortars. Tell me, while this attack was underway with artillery, tanks and mortars, was there any response from the other side? Was it an exchange of fire? Or was it just the JNA that fired at the village without any firing in response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no return fire. That's why I underlined there was no fighting for the liberation of Lovas. There was just an attack on Lovas and no response from our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have 65 ter 418 - this is tab 16 - on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This document is dated 28 September 1991. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I see the document. I have not seen it before. But I saw similar writing in both Lovas and Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, this document pertains to Bapska. During this time when you were in Ilok, were you presented with any documents from Bapska?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any documents from Bapska, but I saw a similar document, also handwritten, about the surrendering of weapons. Lovas was given that demand verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you say you think you saw a similar document, was that document related to Bapska or some other village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 365 on the screen. This is tab 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This document is not tendered, Mr. Olmsted, the one on the screen -- still on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I would like to tender it. Let me ask him one more question. Maybe we can have at least some foundation on it. Since he doesn't, at this time, recognise this one, per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It mentions in the first paragraph that ZNG, Croatian MUP, and armed civilians in Bapska were in the area. To your knowledge, did Bapska have any Croat armed forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. There were just civilians and civilian guards in our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that you were issued with an ultimatum or demands in Lovas and I think you mentioned other places. What happened in Bapska? Were they also issued with an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The pattern of behaviour was the same. First, there were obligations and ultimatums given that could not be met, and that was a pretext for the JNA and/or paramilitaries to attack that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be tendered at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object to admitting of this document because there is no nexus between the witness statement and this document. The witness said that he hasn't seen this document, and he doesn't know the elements contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, when I asked you whether you wanted to tender this, I didn't mean that as a trap. But, indeed, in -- in -- at first sight, there seems to be a nexus problem. You were asking for another document before I -- I -- I asked you whether you would tender this one. Is that a similar one, the one you wanted to have on the screen after this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. It's something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Completely different. And what is your response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the Defence is not taking the position that every document shown a witness, the witness must have seen that document at a particular time, as they've certainly shown a number of documents to witnesses that they've never seen. Our position is this witness was aware there was an ultimatum. He was aware of the situation. As far as armed Croats in Bapska, he was speaking to people from Bapska in Ilok, and so this gives enough of a nexus for it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection -- the objection is overruled; Judge Mindua dissenting. So the document may be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P316. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 365 on the screen. This is tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, this is an order issued by the command of the JNA 1st Infantry Mechanised Guards Division, dated 4 October 1991. If we could just go to the last page. We can see that these orders are issued by Major-General Dragoljub Arandjelovac. Now, I don't want you to go into any details right now, but did you meet this General in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I did. On the 11th, in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was that the 11th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 11th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can go to page 1 of the original; page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look under item number 4 of this order, the General orders the 2nd Infantry Motorised Guards Brigade to take control of the villages of Bapska and Sarengrad by engaging one armoured battalion, a 122-millimetre Howitzer battalion and anti-aircraft defence, light self-propelled artillery rocket battalion in co-ordination with the Territorial Defence special forces. Can you tell us, how does this type of artillery listed here compare to that which was used on Lovas in early October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I believe that an identical artillery force attacked Lovas and the neighbouring villages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it mentions Territorial Defence special forces. Can you give us any insights into what kind of forces those were?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Those were the forces that I referred to as paramilitaries. They called them territorials and we called them paramilitaries. They were supposed to be linked to the JNA. They said that they were not, but I think that they were. I'm sure that they were linked to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall assigned Exhibit Number P317. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I now want to move onto this meeting that you attended on the 11th of October with the JNA. Can you tell us, who from Ilok attended that meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, we were headed by a JNA officer, Grahovac. There was myself, Katica Coric, Stjepan Kraljevic, Mayor Mrsic, Boro Magovac, there must have been somebody else, but this is all I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where in Sid did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In Sid, in the school near the park, in the centre of Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that the same school that you attended meetings with the JNA over Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was a different school. The first one was close to the fair-grounds, in the western part of Sid, whereas the latter was in the centre of Sid, very close to the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that General Arandjelovac was present at that meeting. Who else from the JNA was present?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: There were some other officers and the JNA troops that escorted us and kept guard in the very room where the meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at this meeting did General Arandjelovic make any demands on the residents of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just like Petrovic told us, Arandjelovic told them that they should hand over weapons, that they shouldn't open fire on the military because they were capable of razing Ilok to the ground within the scope of a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did the General say would happen if Ilok refused to surrender its weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, they threatened to attack Ilok and level it with the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how did the Croat delegation -- delegation from Ilok respond to this threat?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I believe that the mayor of Ilok, Mrsic, said that there were some 12.000 people in Ilok, including a lot of women and children, and that if something like that should happen, it would result in a major massacre for which, sooner or later, somebody would be held responsible. To which the General responded, I am a soldier, and all -- all I do is carry out my military tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ask the General anything about Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: At the end of that meeting, I asked him about Lovas. I told him, General, sir, and he said, No, I'm not a sir, I'm a comrade. I told him Lovas had been attacked the day before, 21 people were killed, and some 20 people -- houses were set on fire. And he said, The military didn't do that. And I said how -- what do you mean? I saw them wearing military uniforms, and at the end of the day, paramilitary units did not have that kind of artillery weapons. And then he said that we had killed a member of the Territorial Defence. I suppose he meant Djordjevic, and then I said -- or, rather, he said that a member of the Territorial Defence was killed in the field, and then I told him that Zelimir Petrovic knew very well, because we had agreed to that, that whatever might have happened outside of the village, in the field, that we shouldn't be held responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: And then he called the meeting off abruptly and said, We're done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 403. This is tab 11. This is agreement dated 11 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it because I attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who drafted this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The agreement was drafted by JNA representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I take it from your earlier answer that the JNA presented you with this agreement at that meeting in Sid?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Not to me personally, but they showed it to the representatives of Ilok who then, in their turn, showed it to me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in -- item 1 mentions paramilitary organisations. Were there any such organisations in Ilok at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In Ilok? On the Croatian side? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any Croat armed forces in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The Croatian police was in Ilok because there was a Croatian -- there was a police station in -- in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there a local TO as well?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: There was a Crisis Staff in Ilok and there were also people who were on the guard detail, just like in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In Ilok, people mostly had hunting rifles, and there were a few Kalashnikovs, or automatic rifles. The Ilok police had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I see the time, Mr. President. I'm not quite done with this document, but maybe we should break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, we take the second break. Come back at 12.45. You will be escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, I'd like to return to this document that we were talking about before the break. And if you could look under item number 6, it states that: "A JNA unit will occupy the town and establish a town command, thus securing peace until the situation becomes stable." Given about what you knew about the situation in Ilok at the time, was it necessary for the JNA to come in to establish peace and stability in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: There was no need for that. It was peaceful and stable. Nobody had to establish anything. Nobody had to come and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At this stage, after this meeting with the JNA in Sid, what level of trust did the Ilok delegation have that the JNA would comply with this agreement or any other agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, there was very little trust that things would be honoured, given what had happened in Tovarnik, Bapska. It was a signal that similar things would happen in Ilok as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how was it decided whether or not to sign this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was agreed that a referendum should be organised to enable the citizens to express their will as to how things should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall what date that referendum took place?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was on the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P318. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have up 65 ter 404. This is tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a voting slip. Do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this slip.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: This is about collectively moving away due to the crisis situation, whether we are in favour or against, and whether we were in favour of handing over all weapons and signing an agreement with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So were these the two questions that were put to the Ilok population?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, this concerns Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see that the alternative to signing the agreement with the JNA to surrender weapons was to move out of Ilok. Other than these two options, were any other options discussed?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was either/or. Either to stay, or to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But there was no third option?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall assigned Exhibit Number 319. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 413 on the screen. This is tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a report on the 13 October referendum. And we see on page 1 that the Ilok population voted against turning in their weapons. And if we turn to page 2, we see that they also voted to move out of Ilok. Does this accurately reflect the outcome of that referendum?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The result reflected here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What did you and the other Croats in Ilok believe would happen in you remained in Ilok and did not move out?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, based on the previous developments in Lovas, Bapska, and Tovarnik, when paramilitary units entered those villages and terrorised the population and even killed people, those of us who were in Ilok, including the citizens of Ilok, and those of us who found shelter in Ilok, decided that the best thing for us would be to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P320. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After this referendum, did a part of the Ilok population leave the region?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. A majority. Almost all refugees and a lot of the Ilok population left the area on the 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about you?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did you all go?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We formed a column. We left around 10.00. The column was several kilometres long. We went along the bridge in Backa Palanka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the names of all the places, once again, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If could you repeat the names of the places, the villages that you mentioned. The translators did not get them.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Very well. We set out from Ilok at 10.00. In front of the bridge near Backa Palanka we were controlled by the JNA. We proceeded towards Sid. From Sid, we went to Adasevci, and from Adasevci we went to the Zagreb-Belgrade highway. And then in the village of Lipovac, we crossed over to the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what were you allowed to bring with you, you and the other refugees allowed to bring with you, or able to bring with you, when you left Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We were allowed to bring our personal belongings, or those who had vehicles could drive their own vehicles away, and they could load those vehicles with their personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Given the situation, how much personal belongings was an average person able to bring?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: What you could fit into nylon shopping bags. Some clothes, some footwear. That's what we all had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2214 on the screen. This is tab 20. These are excerpts from a book of minutes of the Ilok Municipal Assembly from 1991. If we could turn to page 3 in the original; page 5 of the English. And what we have in front of us are minutes from a meeting held on 11 October 1991 of the Expanded Session of the Ilok Assembly. And in it, we see that they discussed an earlier meeting with General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you've had a chance to look at these minutes during proofing. Can you confirm, the information contained here about the meeting that you attended on 11 October in Sid, is this information consistent with what was discussed at that meeting in Sid?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what we discussed and agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 4 of the original; page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a portion of minutes from a 12 October meeting of the Ilok Assembly and the minutes reflect that someone by the name of Salihovic said that it was "out of the question for anyone to leave Ilok with weapons." It says: "The General said this explicitly yesterday. What's more, he said if anyone or anybody was to shoot from the column, they will target the column." Who was Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Salihovic was a local, a local and a member of the municipal assembly of the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall whether General Arandjelovic issued this warning at the 11 October meeting in Sid?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He said that if anything happened, if anybody opened fire on the military at any point in time, if fire came from the column, the military would retaliate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, what is meant by "column" here? Column of what?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The column of refugees who left Ilok and proceeded towards Sid and then further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 5 of the original; page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see these are minutes from a 12 October 1991 assembly meeting in Ilok. And we see that D. Bosnjak noted that Rendulic from Lovas passed on a message that there were -- are around 1.000 persons for the moving out. Which Rendulic is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Me. I said that all the refugees from Lovas who were at that point in time in Ilok wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, the thousand persons that are referenced here, those are citizens of Lovas who came to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mainly the residents of Lovas who came to Ilok and wanted to get out of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would object to -- to it because there is no complete minutes from these meetings but just extracts prepared by Stjepan Kraljevic and some other person. I think that it should be provided -- that whole -- the entire minutes from these meetings should be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do they exist, the entire minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is what we have. Of course, if we had the entire minutes, we would certainly not only have disclosed them to Defence but we would probably be using them here today. They are what they are. They are extracts. The Trial Chamber is aware that they're extracts, and the witness was able to speak to a number of entries in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P321. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I now would like to play a video for you. This is 65 ter 4874.1. We'll bring it up on Sanction and we have a transcript for it. So we'll let that play.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we pause it. I don't hear a translation. At least the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]: Anchor: We are moving to Slovenia and Western Srem. "Reporter: After the press conference, dear viewers, which was held in Erdut today, we asked Goran Hadzic, president of the Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, to answer some questions for the viewers of Television Belgrade. Mr. Hadzic, to what extent is the fighting going on in this theatre of war, serious and fierce? What are the prospects? "Goran Hadzic: The fighting is intense. This first operation, the first part, meaning the liberation of Western Srem, is in its final stage. As I said, fighting for Vukovar is ongoing. We can say that our units control nearly 50 per cent of the city. We have secure positions and are advancing house by house. The action of mopping up Ustasha villages was also carried out in the last two days. Following the mopping up of Sid-Vinkovci section, a couple of Ustasha villages in this section of the central part of our region were mopped up three days ago. Bogdanovci and the villages over there. Some villages are surrendering. In Ilok, specifically, one wing offers to surrender, while the other extreme wing will not let them. I will have talks regarding this today so they can surrender their weapons and perpetrators can be held responsible before the law, whereas the innocent can stay and live with us. "Reporter: Is the territorial army, the defenders of the villages, the Yugoslav People's Army, going to launch a stronger offensive because, as you are aware, there is talk about a great number of complaints with regard to intensive war operations, especially by the JNA? "Goran Hadzic: Well, yes, there are complaints. They are relatively justified, I would say, given the attitude and the possibilities. Our goal is not the mass killing of Croats but punishing individuals in their midst. This means we have tried everything through democratic and other peaceful means to prevent this. However, even after the signing of the truce, agreements, and negotiations, the Ustasha continue disregarding what they signed. It means that everyone with this -- I mean, I don't trust them at all. This is clear to me. There can be no negotiating with them and the situation has to be resolved militarily. The communique of the Supreme Command speaks to this effect, but we have to be aware that the army cannot carry this out without the people. So we will have to have some co-ordinated action, real co-ordinated action between the people and the army. "Ratko Jerman, a volunteer for Donji Radici village, was killed. We are moving to Slavonia and Western Srem ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify the man wearing the camouflage uniform in this interview?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise him. That's Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recognise the building he is standing in front of?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I recognise the building. That's a building in Erdut, near the winery.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in this interview, Mr. Hadzic states that: "The action of mopping up Ustasha villages was also carried out in the last two days. Following the mopping up of Sid-Vinkovci section, a couple of Ustasha villages in the section of the central part of our region were mopped up three days ago." What region is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He is talking about the area that includes these villages that had been occupied by the JNA and the paramilitaries, Lovas, Bapska, and further on, and from these villages, Croats were mainly driven out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He mentions that: "In Ilok, one wing offers to surrender while the other extreme wing will not allow it." Were there two wings, or factions in Ilok on this issue?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I believe there were no two factions. You could see from the referendum that most of the population was in favour of moving out. There were really no two opposing factions. There was nobody who was preventing people, trying to stop them from leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there any faction that was in favour of armed conflict or of entering armed resistance against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No way. We knew much in advance, looking at the forces that occupied Ilok, that we did not stand a chance. Nobody had enough strength to oppose the JNA and the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic then states: "I will have talks regarding this issue," referring to Ilok, "today, so they can surrender their weapons and perpetrators can be held responsible before the law ..." What perpetrators is he referring to there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I have no idea whom he had talked to, whether he talked to anyone. But there were no forces there, there was no need to talk to anyone about their moving out. I think it was posturing. They needed to paint this false picture, that those were Ustasha villages, and that they needed to drive out the Croats because they were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you, while you were in Ilok or leaving Ilok, did you learn about the presence of any members of the Croat/Serb leadership who were in the area during these events?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about -- what about on the bridge leading out of Ilok on the day of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: At the exit, there were JNA troops, and I was told there was a -- the mayor of Vukovar, Slavko Dokmanovic, but I didn't see him myself. Other people told me, How could you fail to see Slavko? And in fact, I knew Slavko from before but I did not recognise him. There were too many people in uniform. Whereas other people did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you say other people saw him, what other people saw him?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: People from Ilok who knew him well. He occupied a prominent position once in our municipality. He was the agricultural inspector and later he was president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this video-clip be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit Number P322. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And finally, I want to call up on the screen 65 ter 5085. This is tab 32. And if we could not broadcast this one as it is subject to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, while this is coming up on the screen, if you could just answer this question I have. You told us, Mr. Rendulic, about the events in Sotin, Tovarnik, Lovas, Bapska, and Ilok. Did you observe any patterns in the way that events unfolded in all of these villages?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Well, I said a moment ago and earlier in my evidence that I believe it was all the same pattern, the same scenario. To put pressure on these Croatian villages, to so panic with an initial artillery attack, and then allow the paramilitaries to enter these villages, to go on a rampage, to burn houses, kill people, instilling even more fear. And the pressure from the JNA and the paramilitaries was intentionally so strong with one objective only: That Croats leave those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of the English version of this document; page 5 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see under Roman numeral II there are conclusions in this report about a JNA scenario, how it often evolved along the following lines. And then it gives six points, sub-points, the first being tension and confusion and fear is built up. Secondly, there's artillery or mortar shelling. Third, there's an ultimatum by the JNA regarding the collection of weapons. And, fourth, without waiting for the results of the results of ultimatum there is a military attack. Fifth, at the same time, or shortly thereafter the attack, Chetniks enter the village and finish the job. Is this description provided in this report consistent with what you observed?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is almost 100 per cent consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under item 5 it states that the Chetniks enter the village to finish the job. Did you arrive at any conclusions why the JNA did not itself go in as an infantry into these villages after the artillery attack? Why did they send in paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: The JNA was supposed to play a milder role, to keep a low profile, to refrain from directly participating in the expulsions and attacks on those villages, to protect its own image. However, they were in cahoots with paramilitary units to provide artillery support first and launch the initial attack because, of course, the paramilitaries did not have artillery, and then after the artillery attacks, the paramilitaries, Chetniks, and Seselj's Men and others would be allowed to go in to go on a rampage, to create havoc, and kill and burn. And that's how the panic was sowed and people were intimidated and made to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under item 6 of the report it mentions that: "Ilok was not destroyed; as in this stage, it represents an asset with a fundamental value." Could you tell us, what would the fundamental value of an undestroyed Ilok have been for the JNA or the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I think that the JNA, the Serb forces, needed one town to remain standing. Vukovar was destroyed. There were too many destroyed cities and towns already, and if they destroyed everything, they would be simply left without any accommodation. That's one reason. And, second, Ilok is on the juncture between Vukovar and Backa Palanka one way and another way towards Sid. So they needed one town to remain standing but vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could just turn quickly to page 12 of the English; page 14 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we can see this is an account of the attack on Lovas given by refugees to this international organisation. And it mentions in it, 15 machine-guns were collected in response to the JNA's demands. Were there any machine-guns in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, there were no machine-guns whatsoever. All there was, was light weaponry. Machine-guns are infantry weapons, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think had you an opportunity to look at this report. Other than that, is the rest of the information provided by these refugees generally consistent with events in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me look at this. Yes, that's mainly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P323, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Rendulic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I represent Mr. Goran Hadzic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, first of all, I want to make a correction to certain errors in the record. One of them is on page 33, where you discussed the attack on Tovarnik by the JNA. And, as far as I heard you, you said that, among other things, both churches were hit. You meant the Orthodox church and the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because only the Catholic church is on the record. It must be a mistake. Because truth to be told, you spoke very fast. The other thing is on page 34. It concerns your conversation with Major Radisavkic. I think at one point he told you, complaining about the general devastation and destruction, he said, Why is Europe silent? Why don't they do something? Did he say that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us before that for many years you had worked at the co-operative in Lovas before the war, and the last five years before the war started, you were the director, the general manager of that co-operative.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That co-operative must have wielded great influence in a small place like Lovas. It must have been very important.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: To its economy, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were on good terms with all the residents of Lovas, weren't you, regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Absolutely with everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that, up to 1991, you were a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were many other members of the same League of Communists in Lovas at the time, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me about your reasons for leaving the League of Communists in 1991. Was it of your own free will or not?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: You see, at that time in 1991, the activity of the League of Communists was petering out. It all moved to the SDP, the Social Democrat Party. There was no League of Communists anymore, for all practical purposes. So I decided to simply quit. I did not make any grand moves to quit. I just stopped being involved. There was no activity anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not see the SDP as some sort of successor to the policy of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I did not want to join the SDP or the HDZ. I simply wanted to get out of politics altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the HDZ, you must know that it was founded as a political party in 1989.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of influence that party had in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It did have influence, mainly in achieving independence for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it have many sympathisers in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say there were many HDZ followers in Lovas, my information and my understanding is that everyone there was Croat.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were aware of the circumstances in Lovas, you knew that place well, did you ever wonder why the Serbs were not joining the HDZ? Was it prohibited or did they just not want to?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was not prohibited. I often talked to them about it. What they minded is that the HDZ advocated Croatia's independence and secession from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to understand why it mattered to them so much, the people to whom you talked? Why did it matter to them whether they were going to live in Yugoslavia or independent Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know the real reasons. All I know is that they withdrew at a certain point completely. Even the Serbs who were in the highest bodies of administration at the co-operative, they just quit. They stopped coming to meetings. When I asked why, they pleaded illness or other reasons. They excluded themselves from all the developments, at the co-operative and in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When approximately did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Practically the moment when the HDZ came into power and when the Croatian state was established. That caused widespread discontent among them. But in Lovas specifically, they had absolutely no reason to fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say when the HDZ came into power. That means just after the elections.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, when the HDZ won the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that they won by a majority in Lovas as well.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that the Serbs who lived in Lovas at that time were fearful that Croatia would secede, that Yugoslavia would be no more?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In my view, there was no reason for them to fear that, but some of them did say it in so many words. They said they wanted to go on living in Yugoslavia. It would make them feel better. Old and young said the same. I was not surprised to hear it from older people, but I was surprised to hear it from the younger people. It showed to me that they had been indoctrinated against an independent Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say you were not surprised to hear it from older people. To hear what?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: You know the stories from the Second World War. Older people knew about the Second World War, and what happened and what the situation was then, but younger people did not know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you know that older people knew that, you mean they were contemporaries. They knew first-hand about the crimes committed in the Second World War by Ustashas against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: There were other crimes. There were crimes by Chetniks and partisans against those who were not partisans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain a little? Were the older Serb people afraid that Ustasha crimes would be repeated or other crimes, such as partisan crimes?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe they were thinking that something like that might happen again when the Ustashas come into power. Maybe that's what they said to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not expect the younger people to know that? They must have heard it from their parents, their fathers.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Because I believe that younger people were brought up in a different spirit, in a different culture, with a different world view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were brought up also in a Yugoslav spirit, you will admit.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they were taught different things at school. They were supposed to look at life and the world with different eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You made a distinction a moment ago - that's on page 8 of today's LiveNote - you said that the majority of the Serb population in Lovas were people who were resettled from Banja and Kordun after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, did it have any influence on their attitude?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't think why it should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Banja and Kordun were part of the independent state of Croatia in World War II, you will agree?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were concentration camps nearby, such as Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: We all know that. We learnt our history.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have had occasion to hear in this courtroom that there was not a single Serb family in Croatia that did not have close family perish in those camps.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I cannot talk about that. I don't know whether every Serb family had lost people. Everybody lost something. My father told me how the Croats faired at Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a committee of the Croatian Democratic Union was founded in Lovas in March 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, but I don't know when exactly. I was not a member, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who members were?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Lovas is not a big place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the members of the Executive Committee of the HDZ in Lovas were?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I know that Jozo Milas was the president of the HDZ board. I know that Mujic was a member. His first name was either Ivan or Franjo. I don't know. At that time I did not know much about the policies of the HDZ or its Executive Board. I didn't get involved much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was elected as the president of the municipal assembly in Lovas after the HDZ victory?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Up to then it was a Croat, Jakob Poljak. I can't remember who was elected as president. I know that it was Jakob Poljak before that, and thereafter, I really ... the municipal assembly, is that what you're asking me? The assembly of the local commune?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: It was Jakob Poljak before that, and after that, I don't know who was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and jog your memory. Does Zeljko Cirba's name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Of course, it does. He was employed in my company. I really don't know that he was appointed as the president of the local commune. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have heard that in the second half of April 1990, the HDZ started setting up a military organisation. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, but I don't think it did. How the HDZ could have formed a military organisation at that time? Are you referring to the Lovas HDZ? I don't know anything about that, and I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You -- you know, however, that the president of the HDZ board in Lovas was Milas, right, Jozo Milas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the vice-presidents were Marin Vidic Bili and Josip Grcanac?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I know that they were HDZ members. I don't know what their positions were. I was not a member, as I've already told you, and I repeat it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Josip Grcanac was the chief of the police administration in Vinkovci for a while?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the war he was the chief of the police administration in Vinkovci. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And before the war?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Before the war, he was in Vukovar. But I don't know whether he was chief there. I know that he was a police employee in Vukovar, but I don't know what his position was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that when it comes to the HDZ board in Lovas, Mijo Kolic was a member?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I know he was an HDZ member but I don't know whether he was a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Franjo Krizmanic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Krizmanic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know that he was a member. He is Franjo's son and it is possible that he was also an HDZ member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Josip Badanjak?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He was a member. I don't know what his position was. I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Josip Filic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He was an HDZ member as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And was his nickname Duka?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody was known by that nickname in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ivo Madzarevic, what about him?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: He was an HDZ member as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tomislav Rendulic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Franjo Mujic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Him as well. He was also an HDZ member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Keser known as Braca?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Keser, Braca. I believe his first name was Mile and he was also an HDZ member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, starting with 1990, people in Lovas started arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1990.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that. I don't know that people started getting armed in 1990. If anything was happening on a large scale, I'm sure I would have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have - maybe you know something about that - that in 1990, on the border crossing with Hungary, certain people were arrested, Mile Jovanovic, Josip Mirkovic, Mustafa Mumin, due to the illegal import of weapons and their sale in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I've heard stories but I don't know whether that really happened or not. I just heard rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that training was organised for HDZ members from Vukovar municipality including Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, that didn't happen in Lovas. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Federal Youth Work Campaign?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what happened at the Vupik farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was some sort of military training organised there?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the ZNG members were there, when they had already become a legal Croatian military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they were trained there?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: They were there. I don't know whether they were also trained there, that there was some sort of training organised there. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that we have, the military organisation of the HDZ, that started in the second half of 1990 -- or, rather, in the second half of April 1990, when a decision to that effect was taken. That decision was taken at a meeting in the village of Bogdanovci. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it. I was not at all familiar with that village. I hardly knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that we have, furthermore, it was decided to set up three services within that military organisation. One would be a technical service; the second would be a military service; and the third would be a medical service.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't know that. I don't know whether that was decided there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to some other information that we have, people -- the people who attended and represented Lovas at that meeting subsequently implemented the decision that were taken at that meeting and organised those same services in the village of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't know that. That may well have been the case. However, at that time, no activities to that effect took place in Lovas. Nothing that could be tied to any such services.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the same information that we have, the head of the technical service in Lovas was Ivo Madzarevic. And the task of the technical service was to arm HDZ members.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Ivo was in that position or not. I only know that there was no arming going on at that time. Where would the arms come from in the first place? Nobody had weapons at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were some measures taken in order to obtain weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In 1990? No. Not in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: In 1991, when the situation surrounding Borovo Naselje escalated, we were thinking that we needed security and we could not get that security if we could not defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How was that done, how were weapons obtained?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC
utterances.text: I know that individuals would go to Sid. They would buy hunting rifles and pistols there, legally, against a licence. I believe that the HDZ in 1991, after the May event, they received three or five Kalashnikovs from the police. But the army gave that to the HDZ and the HDZ then was allowed to distribute those weapons. But that was a different time, and some unpleasant events had already started by then. That was in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.
